overview: The Databricks SQL Editor (Query Editor) is the browser-based workspace for writing and running ANSI SQL against Delta tables in the lakehouse, executed on a SQL Warehouse.
It bundles a schema browser, query history, inline visualizations and dashboards, query parameters, and scheduled queries with alerts into a single analyst-facing tool.
It is the primary SQL interface of Databricks SQL (DBSQL), letting analysts explore, transform, visualize, and operationalize queries without writing notebook code.
learningObjectives: Understand what the SQL Editor is, how it relates to a SQL Warehouse, and what data it queries.
Learn its core features: schema browser, query history, visualizations, dashboards, parameters, scheduled queries, and alerts.
Know how to write parameterized, governed ANSI SQL and operationalize it with schedules and alerts.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: The Databricks SQL Editor is a web-based query authoring and execution environment within Databricks SQL that submits ANSI SQL statements to a selected SQL Warehouse for execution against Unity Catalog-governed Delta tables, and provides metadata browsing, result visualization, dashboarding, parameterization, scheduling, and alerting on top of those queries.
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: It is the place in Databricks where an analyst types SQL, picks an engine (a SQL Warehouse) to run it, browses available tables on the left, sees results as a table or chart, and can save the query, turn it into a dashboard tile, parameterize it, schedule it to refresh, and get alerted when a result crosses a threshold.
coreConcept.historicalContext: Released as part of Databricks SQL (DBSQL) around 2020-2021, the SQL Editor was Databricks' answer to traditional SQL workbenches (like Snowflake's worksheets or Redshift query editor). It brought a familiar analyst-friendly SQL experience to the lakehouse so BI users would not need notebooks, and it has steadily added query history, parameters, scheduling, alerts, and a dashboarding layer.

whyItMatters.business: Lets analysts self-serve insights directly on lakehouse data, shortening time-to-insight and reducing dependence on engineering for every report or dashboard.
whyItMatters.engineering: Provides a standard SQL surface with governance and lineage, so analyst queries are auditable and reuse the same Delta tables engineers build, avoiding data copies.
whyItMatters.scalability: Because execution happens on autoscaling SQL Warehouses, the editor scales to many concurrent analysts without the editor itself being a bottleneck.
whyItMatters.cost: Sharing one auto-stopping warehouse across saved/scheduled queries avoids dedicated per-user compute, and result caching makes repeated runs cheap.
whyItMatters.reliability: Query history and saved queries create a reproducible, auditable record; scheduled queries and alerts operationalize monitoring with consistent execution.

coreComponents.name: Schema Browser
coreComponents.definition: A left-hand panel that lists catalogs, schemas, tables, and columns available through Unity Catalog.
coreComponents.purpose: To let analysts discover and reference data without memorizing names or running SHOW commands.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Surface catalog/schema/table/column metadata, data types, and quick previews respecting permissions.
coreComponents.examples: Expanding main > sales > orders to see columns like order_id, customer_id, amount.

coreComponents.name: Query Editor and Execution
coreComponents.definition: The SQL text pane plus a warehouse selector and run controls that submit ANSI SQL to a chosen SQL Warehouse.
coreComponents.purpose: To author, run, and save governed SQL against Delta tables.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Send SQL to the warehouse, stream results, support multiple statements, autocomplete, and save/version queries.
coreComponents.examples: Writing a GROUP BY aggregation and running it on the 'bi-prod' Serverless warehouse.

coreComponents.name: Visualizations, Dashboards, Parameters, Schedules and Alerts
coreComponents.definition: Features layered on a query: chart visualizations, dashboard tiles, query parameters/widgets, refresh schedules, and threshold alerts.
coreComponents.purpose: To turn a one-off query into reusable, interactive, operationalized analytics.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Render charts, embed in dashboards, prompt for parameter values, refresh on a cron, and notify on alert conditions.
coreComponents.examples: A parameterized revenue query charted as a bar graph, pinned to a dashboard, refreshed hourly, with an alert if revenue drops 20%.

internalWorking: The analyst selects a SQL Warehouse and types ANSI SQL; autocomplete and the schema browser read Unity Catalog metadata to assist.
On run, the editor submits the statement to the chosen warehouse, which (via Photon) executes it against Delta tables, applying Unity Catalog permissions and recording the run in Query History.

Results stream back to the editor where they can be displayed as a table, rendered as a visualization, parameterized via widgets, pinned to a dashboard, scheduled for periodic refresh, or wired to an alert that re-runs the query and evaluates a condition.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: Analyst -> SQL Editor (schema browser, parameters) -> SQL Warehouse (Photon) -> Unity Catalog (governance) -> Delta tables -> Results -> Visualizations / Dashboards / Alerts
dataFlowWalkthrough: 1. An analyst opens the SQL Editor and selects the 'bi-prod' warehouse.
2. They browse main.sales in the schema browser and reference the orders table in a SELECT.
3. They add a parameter for region so the query can be filtered interactively.
4. Running the query executes it on the warehouse; the result is rendered as a chart and the run appears in Query History.
5. They save the query, pin the chart to a dashboard, set an hourly refresh schedule, and create an alert if revenue falls below a threshold.

keyTerminology.meaning: A named, persisted SQL query (with its visualizations and parameters) stored in the workspace.
keyTerminology.importance: Enables reuse, sharing, scheduling, and dashboarding; the unit of operationalized SQL in DBSQL.

keyTerminology.meaning: A typed placeholder in SQL (e.g., {{ region }}) that prompts for a value at run time via a widget.
keyTerminology.importance: Makes queries interactive and reusable without editing SQL, and underpins dashboard filters.

keyTerminology.meaning: A log of executed queries with duration, status, warehouse, user, bytes scanned, and the Query Profile.
keyTerminology.importance: Core tool for debugging, auditing, and performance tuning of SQL.

keyTerminology.meaning: A scheduled re-run of a query that evaluates a condition on the result and notifies recipients when met.
keyTerminology.importance: Operationalizes monitoring (e.g., data freshness, KPI thresholds) directly from SQL.

importantConcepts.concept: Editor runs on a warehouse, not its own compute
importantConcepts.explanation: The SQL Editor is just an interface; all execution happens on a selected SQL Warehouse. Performance, cost, and concurrency are governed by that warehouse's size and autoscaling, not the editor.

A query parameter ({{ param }}) becomes a dashboard widget, letting viewers filter by date, region, or category without editing SQL; the same parameterized query backs both ad-hoc analysis and the dashboard.

variationsAndTypes: **Ad-hoc query:** A one-off exploratory SQL statement run interactively in the editor.
**Saved/parameterized query:** A persisted query with widgets and visualizations, reused across dashboards and schedules.
**Scheduled query:** A saved query that re-runs on a cron schedule to refresh dashboards or feed alerts.
**Alert query:** A scheduled query whose result is compared to a condition to trigger notifications.
advantages: **Analyst-friendly:** Familiar SQL workbench experience with autocomplete and a schema browser, no notebook code needed.
**End-to-end:** From writing SQL to visualizing, dashboarding, scheduling, and alerting in one place.
**Governed:** Every query respects Unity Catalog permissions and is captured in Query History for audit.
**Interactive:** Parameters and widgets make queries and dashboards reusable and self-service.
**Decoupled compute:** Runs on autoscaling SQL Warehouses, so concurrency and cost are managed independently.
disadvantages: **SQL-only:** No Python/Scala/ML or arbitrary code; complex transformations may still need notebooks or dbt.
**Depends on a warehouse:** A stopped or undersized warehouse adds latency or queuing the editor cannot fix.
**Lighter than dedicated BI:** Visualizations and dashboards are good but less rich than full BI tools like Tableau.
**Parameter/templating limits:** Parameterization is convenient but not a full templating language like dbt/Jinja.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Use the SQL Editor for ad-hoc analysis, building lightweight dashboards and alerts, validating data, and self-service SQL exploration of the lakehouse by analysts.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Avoid it for code-heavy ETL, ML, or streaming (use notebooks/jobs), and for large, version-controlled transformation projects better served by dbt with CI/CD.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: The SQL Editor is like the cockpit of a car: you sit there to drive, see your dashboard gauges, and set cruise control or warning lights. But the engine doing the work is the SQL Warehouse under the hood. The cockpit gives you controls (parameters), instruments (visualizations), a logbook (query history), and automated alerts (warning lights), while the engine actually moves the data.

commonMisconceptions.myth: The SQL Editor has its own compute.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It has none; it always executes on a selected SQL Warehouse. Slow queries are usually a warehouse sizing/queuing issue, not an editor issue.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Dashboards built in DBSQL replace dedicated BI tools entirely.
commonMisconceptions.reality: DBSQL dashboards are great for fast, governed lakehouse dashboards, but enterprises often still connect Tableau/Power BI to the same warehouse for richer visuals; the editor and external BI coexist.

productionConsiderations.scalability: Concurrency scales via the underlying warehouse's cluster autoscaling; many analysts can share one editor experience as long as the warehouse is sized and scaled appropriately.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Saved queries and schedules give reproducible execution; Query History provides an audit trail and the Query Profile aids debugging of slow or failed runs.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: Underlying warehouse retries failed tasks; queries against immutable Delta snapshots are safe to re-run, and scheduled queries retry per their configuration.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Query History (duration, status, bytes scanned, queue time), alert run history, and warehouse metrics together reveal slow queries and capacity issues.
productionConsiderations.security: All access is mediated by Unity Catalog (catalog/schema/table/column/row); the schema browser only shows objects the user can access, and alerts/schedules run as the owner's identity.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Share an auto-stopping warehouse, rely on result caching for repeated runs, and avoid over-scheduling refreshes; consolidate redundant scheduled queries.
productionConsiderations.performance: Write skipping-friendly filters, leverage Photon on the warehouse, and keep underlying Delta tables OPTIMIZE'd/Z-ordered; use LIMIT during exploration to reduce scanned data.

codeExamples.title: Parameterized query for an interactive dashboard
codeExamples.overview: A saved SQL query using a parameter widget so dashboard viewers can filter by region and date range without editing SQL.
codeExamples.code:
-- Parameters {{ region }} and {{ days }} become dashboard widgets
SELECT
  o.region,
  date_trunc('day', o.order_ts) AS order_day,
  count(*)                      AS orders,
  sum(o.amount)                 AS revenue
FROM main.sales.orders AS o
WHERE o.region = '{{ region }}'
  AND o.order_ts >= current_date - make_interval(0, 0, 0, {{ days }})
GROUP BY o.region, date_trunc('day', o.order_ts)
ORDER BY order_day;
codeExamples.breakdown: {{ region }} renders a text/dropdown widget and {{ days }} a numeric widget. At run time the editor substitutes the chosen values, the warehouse executes the aggregation with Photon, and data skipping prunes Delta files outside the date window. The result feeds a chart pinned to a dashboard.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: Daily orders and revenue rows for the chosen region over the chosen number of days, rendered as a bar/line chart and visible in Query History.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Unquoted string parameters cause SQL errors (quote {{ region }} for string columns); over-broad date windows scan too much data; missing SELECT grant in Unity Catalog blocks the table.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Default parameters to a narrow window so dashboards load fast; filter on partition/Z-ordered columns so skipping prunes files; rely on result cache for repeated identical runs.

codeExamples.title: Schedule a query and create a threshold alert
codeExamples.overview: Use the SQL REST APIs to schedule a saved query to refresh and to alert when a KPI crosses a threshold.
codeExamples.code:
# Schedule a saved query to run every hour (cron) on a warehouse
curl -X POST https://<host>/api/2.0/sql/queries/<query_id>/schedules \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $DATABRICKS_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{ "cron": "0 0 * * * ?", "pause_status": "UNPAUSED" }'

# Create an alert: notify if today's revenue drops below 100000
curl -X POST https://<host>/api/2.0/sql/alerts \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $DATABRICKS_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "name": "Low daily revenue",
    "query_id": "<query_id>",
    "options": { "column": "revenue", "op": "<", "value": 100000 }
  }'
codeExamples.breakdown: The first call attaches an hourly cron schedule to a saved query so its dashboard tiles refresh automatically. The second creates an alert that re-runs the query and compares the 'revenue' column against 100000 using the '<' operator, sending notifications when the condition is true.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: The query refreshes every hour and dashboards update; when revenue < 100000, the alert fires and notifies configured destinations (email/Slack/webhook).
codeExamples.commonIssues: Wrong cron syntax (Databricks uses Quartz-style cron); the alert column name must match a result column; the schedule runs as the owner, so the owner must retain table grants.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Avoid sub-minute schedules that strain the warehouse; consolidate alerts that share a query; keep the alert query lightweight (aggregate first) so it runs cheaply.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: A marketing analytics team needs a self-service revenue dashboard that anyone can filter by region and time range, refreshes automatically, and pages the on-call analyst if daily revenue drops sharply.
endToEndExample.inputData: Unity Catalog Delta tables main.sales.orders (partitioned by order_date) and main.sales.regions.
endToEndExample.architecture: The SQL Editor authors parameterized queries that run on a Serverless SQL Warehouse; visualizations are pinned to a DBSQL dashboard; a schedule refreshes them hourly; an alert monitors a KPI.
processingSteps: 1. In the SQL Editor, select the 'bi-prod' warehouse and browse main.sales in the schema browser.
2. Write a parameterized aggregation query with {{ region }} and {{ days }} widgets.
3. Add a bar-chart visualization and save the query.
4. Pin the visualization to a 'Revenue Overview' dashboard and expose the parameters as dashboard filters.
5. Schedule the query to refresh hourly and create an alert if daily revenue < threshold, notifying Slack.
endToEndExample.output: An interactive, governed dashboard that viewers filter without writing SQL, refreshing hourly, with automated alerting on revenue drops.
endToEndExample.monitoring: Query History shows each refresh's duration and bytes scanned; the alert's run history confirms it is evaluating; warehouse metrics confirm capacity.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: Failed scheduled runs are retried and visible in history; queries read immutable Delta snapshots so re-runs are safe; Unity Catalog permission errors surface clearly to the owner.
endToEndExample.finalResult: Analysts self-serve insights on governed lakehouse data, dashboards stay fresh automatically, and the team is alerted to revenue anomalies, all without writing notebook code or duplicating data.

industryUseCases.problem: Non-engineer analysts need self-service, filterable dashboards on campaign and revenue data.
industryUseCases.solution: Parameterized saved queries in the SQL Editor pinned to DBSQL dashboards running on a shared warehouse.
industryUseCases.benefits: Fast self-service insights, governed access, and no data duplication or notebook coding.

industryUseCases.problem: They must detect stale or anomalous data in critical Delta tables and notify owners quickly.
industryUseCases.solution: Scheduled queries plus alerts in the editor evaluate freshness/row-count/threshold conditions and notify Slack or email.
industryUseCases.benefits: Lightweight, SQL-native monitoring without standing up a separate observability tool.

industryUseCases.problem: Recurring operational reports must refresh on a schedule and be auditable.
industryUseCases.solution: Saved, scheduled SQL queries with visualizations, executed on a warehouse and logged in Query History.
industryUseCases.benefits: Reproducible, audited reporting with automatic refresh and consistent governed results.

productionDeepDive.scalability: The editor itself is stateless; scalability comes from the warehouse it targets. For many concurrent analysts and scheduled queries, size and autoscale the warehouse (scale-out clusters) and avoid pointing heavy schedules at the same warehouse as interactive BI.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: Warehouse task retries plus immutable Delta snapshots make queries safe to re-run. Scheduled queries and alerts retry per configuration; saved queries persist independently of any cluster state.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: Backing the editor with a Serverless warehouse gives near-instant, reliable execution; for in-VPC warehouses keep min clusters >=1 during business hours to avoid cold-start latency on interactive queries.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: Saved queries, dashboards, and alerts are workspace objects exportable via API/Terraform; the underlying Delta data is replicated by the cloud provider, so the analytics layer can be rebuilt in a DR workspace.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Aggregate early, filter on skipping-friendly columns, use LIMIT during exploration, lean on Photon and result caching, and keep underlying tables OPTIMIZE'd/Z-ordered. Use the Query Profile to find scans, spills, and skew.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: Share one auto-stopping warehouse across saved/scheduled queries, avoid over-frequent schedules, exploit result caching, and consolidate redundant alerts/queries to reduce warehouse runtime.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: Unity Catalog governs every query; the schema browser only shows permitted objects. Schedules and alerts execute as the owner, so manage ownership carefully and review grants. Audit logs and Query History capture who ran what.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Query History (duration, status, bytes scanned, queue time, Query Profile), alert run history, and warehouse utilization metrics provide full observability of analyst SQL workloads.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Analysts use scheduled queries and alerts to validate freshness, row counts, null rates, and KPI thresholds, complementing upstream Delta constraints and DLT expectations.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: Alerts re-run queries and notify email/Slack/webhook on conditions; audit and system tables log execution. Centralize Query History exports for governance and tuning.

recommendedPractices: **Parameterize reusable queries:** Use {{ params }} so one query powers ad-hoc analysis and dashboard filters.
**Aggregate before alerting:** Keep alert/scheduled queries lightweight by returning small aggregated results.
**Use the schema browser and autocomplete:** Reference correct, governed table/column names to avoid errors.
**Right-size the warehouse you target:** Editor performance depends on the warehouse; pick a Serverless one for instant start.
**Review Query History and Profile:** Diagnose slow queries by inspecting scans, spills, and queue time.
engineeringStandards: Manage important saved queries, dashboards, schedules, and alerts as code via Terraform/API for reproducibility.
Set explicit owners for scheduled queries and alerts and ensure owners hold the necessary Unity Catalog grants.
Establish naming and folder conventions for saved queries and dashboards to keep the workspace navigable.
designRecommendations: Separate interactive analyst warehouses from warehouses serving heavy scheduled refreshes to protect SLAs.
Default parameters to narrow windows so dashboards load quickly.
Promote stable, version-controlled transformations to dbt rather than maintaining sprawling saved queries.
namingConventions: Name saved queries by domain and purpose, e.g., 'sales__daily_revenue_by_region'.
Prefix alerts with the monitored metric, e.g., 'alert__revenue_drop'.
Use consistent parameter names (region, days, start_date) across related queries.
documentationStandards: Document each saved query's purpose, parameters, target warehouse, and owner.
Document dashboards: which queries back which tiles and how filters map to parameters.
Record alert conditions, thresholds, and notification destinations.
testingStrategies: Run queries with edge-case parameter values (empty, max range) to verify correctness and cost.
Test alerts by temporarily lowering thresholds to confirm they fire and notify.
Validate scheduled refresh timing and verify dashboards update as expected.

commonMistakes.mistake: Blaming the editor for slow queries.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Analysts assume the SQL Editor runs the query, not the warehouse.
commonMistakes.impact: Time wasted tweaking SQL when the real issue is an undersized, stopped, or queuing warehouse.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Check Query History queue/run time and warehouse sizing/autoscaling; the editor is just the interface, the warehouse does the work.

commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Parameters look like variables, so analysts write WHERE region = {{ region }} without quotes.
commonMistakes.impact: Syntax errors or unintended behavior for string-typed columns.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Quote string parameters in SQL ('{{ region }}') and choose the correct parameter type (string, number, date, dropdown).

commonMistakes.mistake: Over-scheduling heavy queries and over-creating alerts.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Setting many frequent refreshes/alerts 'just to be safe'.
commonMistakes.impact: Keeps warehouses running, drives up cost, and adds load that slows interactive users.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Schedule only as often as needed, aggregate alert queries, consolidate duplicates, and isolate scheduled load on a separate warehouse.

comparisonSection.explanation: The SQL Editor is the analyst-facing interface for writing, visualizing, scheduling, and alerting on SQL; the SQL Warehouse is the Photon compute that actually executes it. The editor has no compute of its own and always targets a warehouse.

The SQL Editor is purpose-built for analyst SQL with schema browsing, parameters, dashboards, and alerts; a notebook supports mixed Python/Scala/SQL/ML code on clusters and is better for engineering, ML, and complex transformations.

DBSQL dashboards are fast, governed, and native to the lakehouse but offer simpler visuals; external BI tools provide richer visualization and existing enterprise adoption while connecting to the same warehouse and Delta tables.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is the Databricks SQL Editor and what does it run on?
beginnerQuestions.answer: It is the browser-based tool for writing and running ANSI SQL against Delta tables in the lakehouse. It has no compute of its own and executes queries on a selected SQL Warehouse (Photon-powered).
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Stress the separation: editor = interface, warehouse = compute. Mention it queries Unity Catalog-governed Delta tables.

beginnerQuestions.question: Name the main features of the SQL Editor.
beginnerQuestions.answer: Schema browser, query authoring with autocomplete, query history, visualizations, dashboards, query parameters/widgets, scheduled queries, and alerts.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Group them into discover (schema browser), run/debug (history/profile), and operationalize (parameters, dashboards, schedules, alerts).

intermediateQuestions.question: How do query parameters make dashboards interactive?
intermediateQuestions.answer: A parameter like {{ region }} renders a widget; at run time its value is substituted into the SQL. Exposed on a dashboard, the same parameter becomes a filter so viewers can change region or date range without editing SQL, and one parameterized query powers both ad-hoc and dashboard use.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Mention quoting string parameters and choosing the correct parameter type (dropdown/date/number).

intermediateQuestions.question: How do scheduled queries and alerts work together?
intermediateQuestions.answer: A scheduled query re-runs on a cron to refresh dashboards or feed an alert. An alert re-runs a query and compares a result column to a condition (operator + value), firing notifications (email/Slack/webhook) when the condition is met. Both run as the owner's identity.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Highlight keeping these queries lightweight and aggregated, and that ownership/grants matter.

advancedQuestions.question: An analyst says the SQL Editor is slow. How do you diagnose it?
advancedQuestions.answer: Check Query History for that query: separate queue time from execution time. High queue time means the warehouse is concurrency-bound (scale out clusters); high execution time means the query/data is heavy (inspect the Query Profile for scans, spills, skew; OPTIMIZE/Z-ORDER the table; add filters). Also confirm the warehouse is started and Serverless for fast cold start.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Show you know the editor has no compute and that tuning is about the warehouse and the query plan, not the UI.

advancedQuestions.question: When should work move from the SQL Editor to dbt or notebooks?
advancedQuestions.answer: Move to dbt when transformations need version control, testing, modular models, and CI/CD rather than sprawling saved queries. Move to notebooks when you need Python/Scala, ML, streaming, or complex procedural logic the editor's SQL-only surface cannot express.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Demonstrates understanding of the editor's boundaries: great for analyst SQL and lightweight ops, not for engineering pipelines.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: Leadership wants a self-service revenue dashboard, filterable by region and date, refreshing hourly, with a Slack alert if daily revenue drops 20%. How do you build it in DBSQL?
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: One parameterized aggregation query covers both the dashboard and the alert. Parameters become dashboard filters. A schedule refreshes tiles; an alert re-runs an aggregated query and compares to a threshold. Use a Serverless warehouse for instant start.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: Write a parameterized query (region, days) in the SQL Editor on a Serverless warehouse, add a chart, save it, pin it to a dashboard with the parameters as filters, schedule hourly refresh, and create an alert on the revenue column with a threshold/operator that notifies Slack.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design a governed self-service analytics experience for 200 analysts using DBSQL, covering authoring, dashboards, scheduling, and alerting.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Use the SQL Editor for authoring parameterized saved queries on Unity Catalog Delta tables. Serve interactive analysts from a Serverless warehouse (autoscaling for concurrency) and run scheduled refreshes/alerts on a separate warehouse to protect interactive SLAs. Manage key queries/dashboards/alerts as code.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: Separate warehouses cost more but isolate scheduled load from interactive users. DBSQL dashboards are lighter than Tableau but governed and native; allow external BI on the same warehouse for power users. Parameters are convenient but less powerful than dbt/Jinja templating.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Scale interactive concurrency via warehouse cluster autoscaling; keep schedules lightweight and staggered; OPTIMIZE/Z-ORDER underlying tables; use result caching; monitor Query History queue time to decide when to scale out.

keyTakeaways: The SQL Editor is the analyst-facing interface of Databricks SQL for writing ANSI SQL against governed Delta tables, but it has no compute of its own and always runs on a selected SQL Warehouse.
Its features span discovery (schema browser), execution and debugging (query history and profile), and operationalization (visualizations, dashboards, parameters, schedules, and alerts).
Query parameters turn a single saved query into interactive, reusable analysis and dashboard filters without editing SQL.
Scheduled queries refresh dashboards automatically and alerts re-run queries to notify on threshold conditions, giving SQL-native monitoring.
It is ideal for self-service SQL analytics and lightweight ops, but code-heavy ETL, ML, or version-controlled pipelines belong in notebooks or dbt.
